#262 - I’d have to go back at least to the age of 14 (I’m now 41), when my life as I knew it ended for the first time. It is now in the process of doing so for the second time, and it’s clear that the first steps onto my current downward spiral were a result of my acting out in pain and rage, because my old life and all the things I once loved were torn away from me. If the version of me that exists now could have a long, serious conversation with the one back then, I believe I could convince myself of the need to completely suppress all his emotions and personal impulses, from anger to libido to selfish gluttony to general suspicion of society. Instead of a constantly self-destructing introverted narcissist with a sense of principle that’s radically contradicted by our current social order, I would simply become a sociopathically efficient salesman and a fitness enthusiast, totally suppressing all of my desires and only pursuing financial success, to ensure that one day I would own my own home, probably have a wife, maybe even a few children who I could raise with the same wisdom. Sadly, my passion for Sentinels and my general creative impulses would be a casualty of this process, as I would have to completely abandon all recreational self-indulgences, but this is a necessary consequence of growing up, when you can’t count on your parents to provide for your extended childhood forever.

Question of the Day #265: What real-world IP would you want creative control over?

Magic the Gathering, absolutely no question. I could make a few improvements to D&D, but with a couple of exceptions like the recent orc debacle, the 5E team has been doing pretty good work; even the two comic universes probably don’t require my help. But the makers of MTG have dropped more balls than the entire history of the NBA, constantly making short-sighted corporate decisions to push profitability, at the cost of damaging the future of the brand.

I have actually worked for the creative team in a small capacity one time, and I flatter myself that them ceasing to return my calls was a small injustice of this sort. But by far the biggest such fumble, which I would immediately work to correct if I wound up owning the company, involves an individual whom I know only as Mercer, the handle he went by on the MTG Salvation forums a little over a decade ago.

Mercer is a fairly talented artist, probably still working in this capacity, and one of his earliest publicized projects was a webcomic called Nascent. This tells the story of Earth becoming a part of the MTG universe, with people in various IRL countries becoming able to intuitively use color magic in a superpower-esque fashion, and following the first such person to become a Planeswalker, traveling to the other worlds that Magic has published. Not only did Mercer have a very innovative imagination, creating such concepts as a humanoid made out of lightning, a race of intelligent beetles, or a swamp with a dark sky that’s lit from below… but more importantly, he showed a very well layered understanding of how the philosophies associated with the five magic colors actually intersect with realistic human psychology. The planeswalker protagonist has a friend whose White-magic inclinations drive her to beat up some schoolyard bullies and get punished, while another of his friends is a goth who carries a switchblade and threatens to murder people who cause trouble for those who “belong” to him, a scary-acting but ultimately benevolent person who was probably being set up as a tragic villain for his former loved ones.

When Magic put out the first bits of information about what would become the New Phyrexia expansion (which, by interesting coincidence, is also the one I worked on, as well as the yearly core set right after it), he was apparently very annoyed by the revisionist history that was applied to the previous Mirrodin setting in order to set up its transformation into NP. The corporate brand team currently in charge of Magic had already had a well established pattern of disregarding previously established lore in favor of their current “unified vision” of the IP franchise, and this was apparently the final straw for Mercer. Not only did he stop playing Magic, but he also stopped making the Nascent webcomic after about 100 pages, and stopped paying for a website to host it on. Thank all that’s holy, I had saved all but maybe two of these pages on my computer, enabling me to binge-read them all once every couple of years; otherwise they would be lost to me forever, and I would be poorer for the lack of this incomplete but brilliant little story.

So if I wound up controlling Magic’s publisher Wizards of the Coast, or preferably its owner the Hasbro corporation, or at bare minimum the MTG department within WotCo, I would do one thing basically first. I would hire Internet-savvy private investigators to track down the actual identity of Mercer (assuming he didn’t just have a Contact Me on his current website), and then show up in a limo and ask for an hour of his time to talk about an old project of his. After providing a groveling apology on behalf of the short-sighted morons who had previously held the authority now possessed by myself, I would then offer to do whichever of two things he would prefer, at any cost I could pay without immediately being fired by the company for bankrupting my whole department overnight. If he had the time or inclinations to raise his own baby, I’d offer to immediately hire him in a role junior only to mine, with respect to the creative department; I might not agree with all of his ideas, but a level of genius such as he displayed deserved to be supported. Alternatively, if he had forgotten MTG completely and didn’t want to relearn it, I would simply offer to purchase the legal rights to Nascent, ask him to summarize any of his ideas he could remember that didn’t make it into the comic during its lifespan (eg confirming or correcting my suspicion that the Goth teenager would end up becoming a nemesis to the planeswalker hero), and leave him with a good sized pile of money and my assurances that I wouldn’t do the creative equivalent of turning his daughter into a prostitute. I would then republish Nascent immediately as one of Magic’s official tie-in comics, create a tie-in set to represent the “Earth with color magic” setting, and begin recruiting the most talented co-writers and artists I could find, in order to continue the Nascent story after this decade-long interruption. (Hey, Doctor Who and Star Trek both had much longer delays before resuming.)

I would fix and alter and otherwise mess with a bunch of other things as well if I owned MTG, but that’s the big one.

Question of the Day #273: Chaos or Order?

All the more reason for me to prefer dogs, filthy and ungentle peasant that I am.

Order can naturally emerge from within Chaos, whereupon it will either crystallize further or be subsumed again. But Order cannot tolerate the existence of Chaos within itself, and will always work to stamp out every last trace of it. For this reason, I am on Team Chaos 100%. Everyone should have the freedom to say (or, in an ideal world, do) literally anything they please… and then, anyone who doesn’t want to hear it has the freedom to stop up their own ears and avoid listening. That’s the kind of fair and reasonable solution that is permitted to exist within a Chaotic system, whereas Order will always work to try and make everything perfectly harmonious and efficient, ruthlessly exterminating any deviation or disruption to their absolutist ideal. By way of analogy, I would rather have hundreds of terrorists bombing random locations all over the world for no reason whatsoever, instead of just a single fanatical organization which has a deliberate plan to completely wipe out my particular kind of creature. The former might have the higher body count, but imo it is far and away the lesser evil.

Well. It has certainly been a while. It’s been over a month since I’ve last posted a QotD . . .

My humble apologies to everyone for neglecting my Questioneer duties without saying anything like that. Alas, Real Life got pretty busy, as I’m sure you all know it does.

I’ve still been checking this forum and reading new posts quite frequently; I just haven’t had enough time to post much.

I suppose that I might as well make this official: I am officially resigning as Questioneer. The end had to come eventually; it might as well be now.

My humility prevents however me, however, from boasting that my number of QotDs (273) is more than twice the amount any previous Questioneer of this thread has had.

I may, from time to time, post a question in this thread if I have one and lack anywhere else to ask it, but don’t count on it. Of course, this definitely is not a farewell; I expect to still be active and participate in this forum, just not in my former role of Questioneer.

Of course, anyone may appoint themself as the new official Questioneer, if they do desire to. Additionally, anyone is free to post a single question in this thread whenever they like.

In closing, I should like to offer you a question:
When GMing the Sentinel Comics RPG, do you use index cards like the book prescribes?

And for those who have not had the pleasure to GM the SCRPG:
When GMing any RPG, what aids/accessories do you use? Maps and minis? Sound effects? A GM screen?

And for those who have not had the pleasure to GM any RPG:
Why have you not GMed any RPG?

And for those who have not had the pleasure to play any RPG:
Why have you not played any RPG?

I can probably manage a question every day. I’ve both played and gmed many games… I started with Champions, did Call of Cthulhu, got very heavily into World of Darkness, then a fair amount of D&D, and a smattering of other random things. Not the SCRPG though; everything I know about it suggests I wouldn’t care for its “just go with it” style of approach.

I forget what number we were at, so in the grand style of my fellow fascist dictators, I shall declare “Year Zero” and begin the numbering all over again, with Just A Question (JAQ) #1 - Superman with some kryptonite poisoning, Legacy with a dose of Regression Serum, and Captain America with a bad head cold all walk into a bar. What happens?

The_Justifier:

Just A Question (JAQ) #1 - Superman with some kryptonite poisoning, Legacy with a dose of Regression Serum, and Captain America with a bad head cold all walk into a bar. What happens?

Well, it goes without saying that, in traditional superhero fashion, the three would probably fight each-other for one reason or another. My money would be on Cap in that fight, ‘cause he’s the underdog, even with the other two’s handicaps.

After that, I’d bet that they’d all calm down, have a round of vanilla Cokes, and swap stories about their adventures, as well as discuss how great America is, before they started trying to figure out what reality they are in and how to get back to their respective universes, which they’d probably do by having the Last Son of Krypton fly fast enough to pierce the spacetime barrier.

In running the SC-RPG, yes, I do use cards, but I bought dry-erase cards so they can be reused. (I also got the GM kit, which includes a bunch of pre-printed cards. They are awesome!!! )

And the rest of this is probably way more than you wanted, so I’ll apologize now. But I thought your final question deserved a bit of respect.

Over the years, I’ve used all kinds of aids/accessories for various games I’ve run:

  • Minis, including some from Hero Forge (because they are awesome!!! ) and Litko stands to use images of whatever I need instead of spending money / using space on the “real thing”
  • Chessex MEGAMAT (wet and dry erase) that I draw the map on, published/laminated maps (from all kinds of sources), printed-at-home maps (that I cut up and tape back together so they only see what they actually know about - many of my own creation), maps drawn on white boards, digital maps revealed on a TV via computer, digital maps revealed via Fog of World (in Realm Works - although note that they are no longer going to be doing development on RW ), and 3-D constructed maps (to either really sell a major moment or provide better visualization of a non-traditional environment), such as these:

IMG_23201920×2560 330 KB

61920×1440 155 KB

  • Alea Tools for all kinds of uses, but mostly to indicate effects on minis and in combination with the initiative board, below
  • A large, home-made initiative board:
    Initiative_board1920×2560 318 KB
  • A variety of tools for mood music / sound effects, although lately I’ve been exclusively using Syrinscape for that
  • A random NPC generator (originally in Excel but now in Google Sheets) that I created to avoid my own biases around NPC details (e.g., gender, race, names) - The link is a copy that folks can mess with all they like, but it’s always a work-in-progress and since it’s always been just for my use I’ve never cleaned it up or included instructions
  • A workbook we use in our campaign session 0 to ensure everyone is on the same page as to expectations for the game - it’s overkill for most folks, but it’s all things we’ve learned over the years that we have had issues with folks not understanding that ended up impacting our games in a negative way
  • And for atmosphere / effect: Flash paper and flash cotton (to create the effect of something blowing up while RPing as an NPC), candles, red light bulbs (especially for horror-themed games, LED bulbs that can change lights via an app (to really alter a mood at a moment’s notice), and all kinds of physical props and puzzles to challenge and entertain the players:

His name was “Lord von Dartus”, which is one letter away from being an anagram of “Strahd.” I’d say that he’s as much an expy of Strahd as he is one of Dracula. He was a pretty stereotypical Vampire. I may, from time to time, post a question in this thread if I have one and lack anywhere else to ask it.

What is your favourite tabletop roleplaying game campaign setting (aside from the Sentinel Comics RPG, of course) for story and lore reasons, not rules and mechanics reasons?

(Also, remember that game ≠ setting. A single RPG can offer multiple different settings.)

Man I completely forgot I was doing Just A Question. Five questions in five days, and then five weeks without. I wonder if it’s worth bothering to resume after a flop like that.

Anyway, my answer would likely be Glorantha if I had ever read it, just based on how beautiful the book is. But since that’s not on my list so far, I have to pick a different answer. Likely candidates are mostly ruled out by being individual sections of a larger interconnected world, where I love the whole but can’t really isolate how much I like the parts (the obvious example being World of Darkness, which isn’t a setting, it’s fifteen settings that are all semi compatible). And of course I rule out any system which is completely generic and has no setting by default, like Big Eyes Small Mouth, probably the prettiest rpg book I own. So I guess I have to go with the coolest thing that’s left. That would probably be…

Well, while the Justifier is busy being eaten by xxt’Hulish, I’ll answer.

It might be Dungeons & Dragons’ Spelljammer, which is just D&D in SPAAAAACE! It’s just so much nonsense. Suffice it to say that I am very excited for its upcoming book.

Other D&D settings that I particularly like are Dark Sun (post-apocalyptic), Planescape (the Planes of Existence), and Urban Arcana (modern-day Earth).

Of GURPS, I like Infinite Worlds (multiversal cops) and Bunnies and Burrows (rabbits with martial arts and psychic powers).

I also like Call of Cthulhu’s Delta Green, which features an ex-government organisation combating the Mythos.

I’m not very fond of the World of Darkness’s setting. It’s just much too bleak for me.

(Of course, I also love the setting of the Sentinel Comics RPG, but I specifically excluded it from the question because I figure that all of us would choose it.)

I guess we can take that little incident as further proof that my tenure as Questioner isn’t being resumed. Too difficult for me to remember something that doesn’t come with continual prompting. As for the incomplete answer, it was meant to be Nobilis. I have huge issues with the rules and worldbuilding, but in pure creative terms, it actually outstrips the WOD’s Changeling subsets in terms of beauty, tragedy poetic symbolism, and just all around coolness. There are probably settings I would like more, but few of them I’ve actually looked at.

If the WOD is too depressing, you should look at Mummy the Resurrection, which was intentionally designed as a ray of hope in the setting’s typical gloom. Naturally it didn’t sell that well, but my copy is still prominently displayed on a shelf, waiting to see actual play someday. There are a couple others that can be spun much more positively, but Mummy is probably the only one where it’s true as the default.

The_Justifier:

I guess we can take that little incident as further proof that my tenure as Questioner isn’t being resumed.

With great power, there must also come — great responsibility! Worry not, for few can carry the burden of the Questioneer.

I looked a bit into Nobilis and Mummy: The Resurrection. The latter does indeed seem more hopeful than the WoD’s other gamelines (judging by my very limited exposure to them). Plus, I do like Egyptian mythology (as evidenced by my like of Sentinels’ Ra).
